messages.author: a94bf563bce55f38
messages.subject: Beginner questions
parts:
Hello all, I have just started with the r distance package and have managed to achieve some basic results. I have two methodological questions that I'd appreciate some help with:

1 - The data from my line transect has a compass bearing between 0 and 360', to the observation. So there are recorded observations either side of the transect line itself. How should I correctly approach abundance estimation when using a detection function like half-norm? 

2 - For a given transect my data has many visits across a year. How should I best approach this when modelling abundance? Should I run an abundance estimation with data for each given day and take the mean?

Thanks

Anthony

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Beginner questions
parts:
Anthony

Thanks for asking your question to the Distance list.  I recommend you have a look at the lectures and exercises associated with distance sampling at our online workshop:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/
Materials there will help with some of the basics.  But to your specific questions
  • distance and angle measurements in the field.  When using the R package, you'll need to covert those measurements to perpendicular distances from the transect. Here's a bit of code showing the perpendicular distance for an angular distance of 10 units, sweeping through the 360 degrees of the compass
    • distance <- 10  # meters lets say
      for (bearing in seq(1,360,by=5)) {
        radian.bearing <- bearing * (pi/180)
        perdis <- abs(distance * sin(radian.bearing))
        cat(i, d.r, perdis, "\n")
      }
  • multiple visits to a transect:  no universal solution to this, it depends upon what is biologically relevant.  However, it is seldom the case there are sufficient detections in a single day to produce reliable abundance estimates.  It is often the situation that data are pooled across days, then a single estimate is produced from the pooled data; that single estimate is an average of animal abundance in the study area across the visits.  Be sure to adjust the effort when pooling data across visits (effort = line length * number of visits).
